title: Book 4 — Melpomene, Chapter 155
paragraphs: After this, Polymnestus, a respected man among the Theraeans, took Phronime from him and kept her as his concubine. In time a son was born to him from her, a son with an impediment in his speech and a lisp. To him, both Theraeans and Cyrenaeans say, was given the name Battus, though I think some other name was given at first, and he was called Battus only after he came to Libya—taking this surname for himself from the oracle given to him at Delphi and from the rank he had obtained, for the Libyans call a king battos. For this reason, I think, the Pythian priestess, when she prophesied, addressed him so, using the Libyan word, because she knew he would become a king in Libya. When he had grown to manhood, he came to Delphi to inquire about his voice; and to his question the priestess answered:
“For a voice you came, O Battus; but lord Phoebus Apollo sends you out as a settler to sheep-rich Libya,”

as if she had said in Greek, “For a voice you came, O king.” He replied: “Lord, I came to you to inquire about my voice, but you answer me with something else that is impossible, bidding me go as a settler to Libya. With what resources, or with what force of men should I go?” For all he said, he did not persuade her to give him any other answer; and as she kept prophesying to him the same things as before, Battus left while she was still speaking and went back to Thera.
